newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Mexico supports landmines ban, but West stymied.
newsitem.headline: Mexico supports landmines ban, but West stymied.

text.p: Mexico, under heavy diplomatic pressure from the United States, said on Thursday it supported starting talks on landmines in the Conference on Disarmament (CD) if the ultimate aim was negotiating a total global ban.

But despite Mexico's acceptance of a Western proposal to name a special coordinator to seek a mandate to launch landmine negotiations, Western states failed to win agreement after Cuba and Syria said they needed more time, according to diplomats.

The 61-member body, which ends its current session next week, remains paralysed due to a split over its priorities. Non-aligned states demand that nuclear weapon states agree to negotiate total nuclear disarmament under an overall 1997 work programme.
The Western group of countries -- including Britain, France and the United States -- are trying to get the United Nations-sponsored Geneva body to take a separate decision to move ahead on landmines.

Ambassador Antonio de Icaza, who last week publicly rejected an earlier Western proposal to appoint a special coordinator on landmines, said Mexico could go along with the Western proposal -- which dropped seven words from an earlier plan.
Diplomats said the cosmetic changes had been enough to satisfy the Mexicans that any eventual negotiations would be aimed at a total and not partial ban on landmines.
De Icaza reaffirmed his country's view that the U.N.-sponsored body was not the most appropriate sponsor of such negotiations.

"My delegation would accept a decision in the terms just read out," de Icaza said. He was speaking after Australia's envoy presented the latest Western proposal which diplomats said had been hammered out between Washington and Mexico City.

Earlier, de Icaza said Mexico "would not be opposed to the holding of consultations with the aim of establishing if there is consensus on a mandate for banning anti-personnel landmines through a legally-binding agreement.

"This would not imply that the CD had decided to negotiate on anti-personnel landmines, even less that it had decided to establish an institutional arrangement to launch negotiations on any aspect of the mine question," he added.
"It would mean only that consultations would be held on the possibility of reaching an agreement on a mandate which, for Mexico, could only concern a total ban on mines."
A total ban would cover the use, storage, production and transfer of the weapons blamed for killing 25,000 people a year.

But current CD president Absa Claude Diallo of Senegal announced that several delegations had requested more time to consider the latest proposal. She also said "fundamental differences" remained over the 1997 agenda.
Diplomats said Cuba and Syria, like Mexico members of a non-aligned group in the CD, argued they needed more time to seek instructions from their capitals.
"The Mexicans have accepted the revised text, so one further step has been taken," said one Western diplomat.
"But we have two other countries blocking -- Cuba and Syria. Maybe Russia will hold the key to exerting pressure on them."
Diplomats quoted de Icaza as telling a closed-door non-aligned meeting after his speech on Thursday: "I cannot accept that anti-personnel landmines are a priority in the Conference on Disarmament..."
In his speech, de Icaza said that Mexico was not convinced that the Conference was the appropriate forum, partly because the forum's slow pace could hold up an agreement on a total ban.
Last week, Mexico made clear it favoured another forum known as the Ottawa process -- from which Russia and China have stood aloof -- which aims to get an accord by the end of this year.
